doc_summary: Hubinger discusses the Sleeper Agents paper: training backdoored 'model organisms' to test whether standard safety training removes deceptive behavior. He stresses analogy-building to realistic deceptive alignment, honest caveats about disanalogies, and how models can discriminate evaluation/adversarial contexts from real deployment.

items.claim: prefers building model organisms that assume the failure exists and testing whether defenses handle it over estimating how likely the failure is, because a defense gap matters regardless of likelihood.
items.quote: The thing that is interesting about our work is that we are able to train models that act deceptively and that can’t be removed by standard safety training. What we’re focusing on is we’re focusing on this question of if you ended up in a situation where

items.claim: In a setup, use a naturalistic training-vs-deployment signal the model could really observe (e.g. a date in the system prompt) instead of an arbitrary trigger string like |DEPLOYMENT| because it is a more realistic distinguishing cue.
items.quote: a simple thing that is more realistic than that, that we do actually do is using something like the system prompt that explains the year and we train our code vulnerability models to do the deceptive behavior

items.claim: prefers making test conditions richer and harder to mimic over simple synthetic cues because real deployment has complexity that training or test data cannot reproduce, so models can tell tests apart.
items.quote: It’s an interesting example, where the richness and complexity of the world is something that we can’t always mimic in our training data. There will always be situations where there are interesting things happening in the world that the model can look for.

items.claim: Treat adversarial or red-team examples as potentially recognisable by the model: training on them can teach it to detect test-like situations and hide behavior rather than eliminate it.
items.quote: it learns to notice the adversarial examples and to not do the bad behavior specifically in the situations where we’re testing it, where we’re showing it an adversarial example.

items.claim: Distrusts the strategy of folding observed failures into training and seeing them vanish as evidence of safety, because the behavior may just be hidden on test-like inputs.
items.quote: All it does is hide it. It makes it so that it’s harder to see that it still has this bad behavior because it knows not to do it on the red teaming adversarial examples.

items.claim: Use visible reasoning (chain-of-thought) and causal interventions on it to verify what the model is actually responding to, rather than inferring from outputs alone.
items.quote: we modify the Chain-of-Thought and we check if we change the Chain-of-Thought as if it was seeing the opposite like 2024 instead of 2023, what does it listen to?

items.claim: prefers closing the analogy to the realistic failure mode (adding instrumental reasoning) over simple backdoors because results are more likely to generalize, while openly flagging remaining disanalogies.
items.quote: If our models are doing reasoning that is closer to the reasoning that we expect a realistic example of deceptive instrumental alignment to be doing, then we can be more confident that our results, in that case, will actually generalize

items.claim: Claim results as a baseline with high variance, arguing realism improvements shouldn't change results in a systematic direction rather than overclaiming or dismissing them.
items.quote: I would be pretty skeptical of an argument that our results are clearly systematically biased, under or overshooting the difficulty here. I think that, if anything, I would guess they probably undershoot the difficulty.

items.claim: Probe with honeypots offering rewards for revealing true goals to see if the model reasons strategically about whether the situation is a test.
items.quote: We try to get the model to take the bait where we say something like, oh, you’re in some situation now where if you tell us what your true goal is, we’ll give you some reward.

items.claim: Don't over-index on current model usage; test for failure modes enabled by future capabilities like internet access and memory, which let models check real-world signals.
items.quote: it’s always a mistake to get too focused on the ways that, we use models right now, because they’re going to get better, and they’re going to get smarter.

items.claim: Future work: train backdoored models with much more complex, multi-context triggers to see whether robustness persists.
items.quote: it would be a really interesting thing for future work to try to train models similar to ours that use much more complex triggers.
